strengths: The formulation of test-time alignment for discrete diffusion models using twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) is theoretically principled and well-motivated.

The use of a first-order Taylor approximation to construct a factorized, locally optimal proposal distribution provides an efficient way to guide discrete diffusion without requiring combinatorial evaluation over the vocabulary.

The paper thoughtfully addresses the non-differentiability and discontinuity caused by the 'Carry-Over Unmasking' constraint in masked diffusion models via a continuous relaxation (Eq. 16 and Appendix D), accompanied by clear finite-difference intuition.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is very limited. The empirical validation is restricted to a 2D synthetic mixture of Gaussians and binarized MNIST. There is no evaluation on standard benchmarks for discrete diffusion models, such as language modeling (e.g., LM1B, OpenWebText), biological sequence design (DNA/protein), or standard discrete image generation.

Key baselines from prior literature on discrete guidance and alignment are missing from the empirical comparison. While methods like D-CBG (Schiff et al., 2024), continuous-time discrete SMC guidance (Lee et al., 2025), and discrete steering/guidance (Nisonoff et al., 2024; Rector-Brooks et al., 2024) are discussed in the related work, none are quantitatively evaluated against the proposed method.

Quantitative evaluation on the image task is insufficient. On binarized MNIST, the paper only reports classifier reward and shows 20 generated samples for a single class ($y_{\text{target}} = 4$). Standard generative evaluation metrics such as FID/clean sample quality, particle diversity, effective sample size (ESS) progression, and computational overhead/wall-clock time across all digits are omitted from the main text.

The main body of the paper is only four pages long, leaving substantial theoretical derivations and experimental settings in the appendix, while leaving the overall submission underdeveloped for a full-length archival conference track.

The method requires sensitive hyperparameter tuning for masked diffusion models, particularly regarding the tempering schedule and partial resampling threshold, as acknowledged by the authors in Section 4.2.

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing the test-time alignment of discrete diffusion models without retraining.
Sound theoretical derivation of the first-order Taylor approximation for the locally optimal twisting proposal in discrete state spaces.
A thoughtful continuous reformulation (Eq. 16 and Appendix D) to handle the discontinuity induced by the Carry-Over Unmasking condition in masked diffusion models.
Well-written appendix connecting discrete-time Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) with continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) formulations (e.g., recovering Lee et al., 2025).
weaknesses: Extremely limited and toy-level empirical evaluation: Experiments are restricted to a 2D mixture of Gaussians and binarized MNIST. For modern discrete diffusion models—whose primary applications are language modeling, code generation, and biological sequence design (proteins/DNA)—evaluating solely on 2D synthetic data and $28 \times 28$ binary digits is insufficient for a top-tier venue.

Lack of rigorous quantitative benchmarking: On binarized MNIST, results are presented primarily via qualitative grids for a single target digit ($y_{\text{target}} = 4$). There is no quantitative evaluation across all classes, nor standard metrics such as generative quality (FID/likelihood), diversity across large sample pools, or classification accuracy.

Missing comparisons against competitive baselines: The paper does not benchmark against other inference-time guidance or SMC methods for discrete diffusion (e.g., D-CBG / Schiff et al., 2024; Nisonoff et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2025) on any standard benchmark.

High computational cost without runtime or scalability analysis: Differentiating through the denoising network $x_\theta$ via Gumbel-Softmax backpropagation for every particle at every diffusion step incurs significant compute and memory overhead. The paper provides no wall-clock time comparisons, memory footprint measurements, or scalability analysis.

Fragility and sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning: The authors acknowledge that masked diffusion models require careful hand-tuning of tempering schedules (e.g., an exponential schedule $\min(1.05^{T(1-t)} - 1, 1)$), partial resampling ratios, and thresholds to prevent degeneracy or premature unmasking. The absence of adaptive tempering limits practical applicability.

strengths: The application of twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) with locally optimal proposals to discrete diffusion models is a well-motivated problem.

The continuous reformulation of the carry-over unmasking constraint (Eq. 16) paired with Gumbel-Softmax relaxation provides an intuitive way to approximate gradients through the discrete generative process.
The manuscript provides helpful theoretical connections in the appendix linking discrete-time SMC to continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) formulations.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is extremely limited. The experiments are restricted to a 2D synthetic mixture of Gaussians and binarized MNIST for a single target class ($y=4$). Discrete diffusion models are typically benchmarked on natural language processing, protein/DNA sequence design, or at least CIFAR-10. Without realistic benchmarks, it is difficult to judge practical utility and scalability.

Lack of comparison with established discrete guidance and alignment baselines. The paper only compares against a basic approximate guidance baseline and naive SMC proposals, omitting prominent related works such as discrete classifier-based guidance (Schiff et al., 2024; Nisonoff et al., 2024) or existing discrete SMC methods (Lee et al., 2025).
The paper structure resembles an extended abstract or workshop draft rather than a full conference paper (the main text spans only 4 pages, with less than one page dedicated to experiments).
High sensitivity to hyperparameters: for masked diffusion, the method requires a delicate, hand-tuned tempering schedule because unmasking is irreversible, highlighting practical brittleness.
In Appendix D, the gradient analysis is carried out on a modified formulation (Eq. 37) rather than the actual formulation used in the paper (Eq. 16), which the authors note has different gradients.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated framework: The paper provides a clear theoretical grounding for Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) applied to discrete diffusion models, deriving tractable importance weights for both product targets (CFG) and reward-tilted targets.

Sound optimal proposal formulation: Characterising the locally optimal proposal and introducing an amortised network trained via log-variance minimisation (with an auxiliary mean estimator) is mathematically well-grounded and practically effective.

Comprehensive and diverse empirical evaluation: The proposed framework is evaluated across synthetic 2D/MNIST benchmarks, language detoxification/steering, biological DNA regulatory sequence design, and high-resolution text-to-image synthesis (Meissonic and MaskGit).

Consistent scaling behavior: The results clearly demonstrate monotonic performance gains as the particle count increases, substantiating the claim of effective test-time scaling for discrete diffusion models.
weaknesses: Training requirement vs. pure inference-time scaling: The amortised proposal (Propamot), which delivers the strongest empirical gains, requires fine-tuning/training of a proposal model. While this is a valid post-training alignment method, framing the overall work primarily as 'inference-time scaling' can be slightly ambiguous given that the best variant requires dedicated training.

Computational cost and latency analysis: While sample complexity in terms of particle number N is well studied, an empirical analysis of wall-clock time and memory overhead during inference (especially compared to simpler inference baselines like Best-of-N or training-free guidance) is largely missing.

Quality and diversity trade-offs in language modeling: In the language experiment (Table 1 and Table 4), SMCamot achieves near 100% toxicity at the expense of higher perplexity (147.6 vs 121.1) and a substantial decrease in n-gram diversity (Dist-1/2/3 dropping to 44/81/91), suggesting noticeable reward over-optimization.

strengths: Principled and Sound Theoretical Framework: The paper provides a rigorous formulation of Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) specifically tailored to discrete and masked diffusion models. The characterization of the locally optimal proposal and the derivation of the log-variance minimization objective (Proposition 3) provide a solid theoretical underpinning for proposal design.

Practical Solutions for Discrete Diffusion Complexities: The authors tackle real practical challenges in applying SMC to modern discrete diffusion architectures, such as handling rewards defined only on clean data (via Monte Carlo estimation and Gumbel-Softmax), addressing the limitations of ancestor sampling via ReMDM, and handling the non-differentiability / alignment of low-confidence sampling schedules.

Comprehensive and Diverse Empirical Evaluation: The empirical validation spans four distinct domains: synthetic tasks (MoG, binary MNIST), language modeling (toxic generation with MDLM), biological sequence design (regulatory DNA generation), and computer vision (MaskGit on ImageNet256 and text-to-image with Meissonic).

Consistent Test-Time Scaling Behavior: The empirical results demonstrate clear scaling laws with respect to the number of particles $N$, showing systematic improvements in target alignment and sample quality compared to baselines such as standard diffusion sampling and Best-of-N (BoN).
weaknesses: Computational Overhead and Wall-Clock Latency: While the paper shows particle scaling benefits, SMC with $N$ particles increases compute and memory footprint linearly (or super-linearly when incorporating reward model evaluations). A detailed breakdown of wall-clock inference time and memory usage across different particle counts and baselines would make the practical cost-benefit trade-off clearer.

Diversity vs. Reward Optimization Trade-off: As acknowledged in the text, the amortized proposal variant (SMC_amot) exhibits noticeable diversity reduction and mode-seeking behavior (e.g., substantial drop in Dist-1/2/3 metrics in Table 1/Table 4, and sample clustering in synthetic MoG in Figure 2). While entropy regularization is mentioned in Appendix D.1.2, a more systematic discussion on controlling the diversity-fidelity trade-off during test-time scaling would strengthen the paper.

Framing of Amortized Proposal: The paper frames the overall contribution primarily around inference-time scaling, but training an amortized proposal network requires an offline optimization phase over trajectories. A clearer distinction throughout the main text between purely training-free test-time guidance (Prop_grad / SMC_base) and amortized fine-tuning (SMC_amot) would avoid potential confusion.

strengths: Principled and Sound Theoretical Framework: The paper provides a clear and mathematically rigorous formulation of Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) tailored for discrete diffusion models, including both product distributions (CFG) and reward-tilting. The derivation of the locally optimal proposal and the log-variance upper-bound objective (Proposition 3) with an auxiliary baseline is elegant and well-justified.

Practical Solutions for Masked Diffusion: The authors effectively tackle practical hurdles in applying importance weighting to modern discrete masked diffusion models, specifically proposing a coherent modification to evaluate log-likelihood ratios under low-confidence / confidence-based remasking schemes (Equations 45–46).

Broad and Diverse Empirical Validation: The evaluation spans a remarkably diverse suite of modalities and applications, including synthetic 2D/MNIST distributions, language generation (MDLM), biological sequence design (DNA regulatory elements), and image generation (MaskGit on ImageNet and Meissonic for text-to-image).

Effective Test-Time Scaling: The results consistently confirm that increasing the number of particles $N$ leads to monotonic improvements in reward and alignment across different domains, demonstrating the practical utility of SMC for inference-time compute scaling.
weaknesses: Conceptual Tension Regarding 'Inference-Time Scaling' vs. Training: The amortized proposal ($q_\phi$) requires explicit optimization via the log-variance loss, which entails a non-trivial training/fine-tuning phase. Framing the entire approach primarily as 'inference-time scaling' is somewhat misleading, as SMCamot relies heavily on amortized post-training rather than purely test-time computation.

Mode Collapse and Diversity Trade-offs: In several experiments, the high reward achieved by SMCamot comes at the expense of sample diversity and quality metrics. In toxic language generation, SMCamot shows a noticeable drop in n-gram diversity (Dist-1/2/3 drops from 56/92/96 to 44/81/91) and worse perplexity. In DNA sequence design, 3-mer and JASPAR correlation metrics lag behind DRAKES.

Computational Cost and Efficiency Analysis: While SMC reduces reward under-optimization compared to guidance and over-optimization compared to standard RL, running $N$ particles with denoising steps significantly multiplies inference latency and memory footprints. A detailed wall-clock time and memory comparison against rejection sampling (BoN) and fine-tuning baselines would strengthen the empirical claims.

Approximation Quality of Propgrad in Large Discrete Spaces: The first-order Taylor approximation used in Propgrad requires relaxing categorical states into continuous vectors via Gumbel-Softmax or embedding gradients, which can introduce gradient noise or become computationally burdensome for larger vocabularies and reward backpropagation.
